title: Asian Pop Grammy Hopefuls Rise: Who Could Fill BTS’s Void?
body:
The Recording Academy’s decision to add an Asian‑pop performance category to the 2025 Grammy Awards has sparked a flurry of speculation about which artists will become the first nominees. While global megastars BTS and BLACKPINK are effectively excluded—BTS due to its hiatus and BLACKPINK’s recent English‑language releases falling outside the Academy’s “Asian‑pop” definition—five other acts have emerged as the most likely contenders to break through the category’s inaugural barrier.

First on the list is South Korean soloist IU, whose 2023 album “Palette” blended traditional Korean instrumentation with contemporary R&B and pop, earning critical acclaim across both domestic and international markets. IU’s track “Love Poem” not only topped the Gaon chart but also garnered a surge in streaming numbers on platforms like Spotify and Apple Music, indicating a growing global fanbase that could translate into Grammy buzz. Her reputation for lyrical depth and vocal nuance aligns with the Academy’s emphasis on artistic merit, making her a strong candidate for a nomination.

Second, Japan’s J‑pop veteran Kenshi Yonezu has been lauded for his genre‑defying approach, merging folk, electronic, and hip‑hop elements into a uniquely Japanese soundscape. Yonezu’s 2024 single “Lemonade” has dominated the Oricon charts and received extensive airplay on Western indie radio stations, suggesting cross‑cultural resonance. The Recording Academy has previously recognized non‑English language entries—most notably with the 2023 Best Global Music Album win—so Yonezu’s innovative production could capture the attention of voters seeking fresh, boundary‑pushing music.

Third, the Chinese boy band WayV, a sub‑unit of NCT, is positioned as a front‑runner thanks to its hybrid Mandarin‑English catalog and strong presence on YouTube’s global music charts. Their 2024 EP “Phantom” showcases a sophisticated blend of trap beats, synth‑pop melodies, and traditional Chinese motifs. WayV’s strategic collaborations with Western producers, coupled with a robust touring schedule across North America and Europe, have expanded their footprint beyond the typical K‑pop circuit, making them a viable nominee under the new category’s criteria.

Fourth, the rising Thai pop act MILD, known for its synth‑driven anthems and socially conscious lyrics, has captured the attention of both regional and international audiences. Their 2023 album “Midnight Sun” earned a spot on several “Best Albums of the Year” lists in Southeast Asia and has been featured on curated playlists for global audiences on streaming services. MILD’s willingness to address mental health and climate issues through a pop lens aligns with the Academy’s recent push toward socially relevant artistry, bolstering its nomination prospects.

Finally, the Philippines’ R&B sensation Moira Dela Torre, whose soulful ballads have consistently charted on Billboard’s Philippines Songs chart, could become the first Filipino artist to receive a Grammy nod in this category. Her 2024 release “Echoes” blends Tagalog lyricism with lush orchestration, and the song’s viral TikTok moments have propelled it into the top ten on global viral charts. Dela Torre’s emotive vocal delivery and polished production have earned praise from critics who view her as a bridge between Asian pop sensibilities and Western adult contemporary standards.

The exclusion of BTS and BLACKPINK underscores a broader conversation about how the Recording Academy defines “Asian pop.” While BTS’s hiatus and BLACKPINK’s all‑English tracks fall outside the stipulated parameters—specifically the requirement that at least 51 percent of the composition be in an Asian language—the new category still offers a platform for a diverse array of artists who blend regional sounds with mainstream appeal. Industry insiders suggest that the Academy’s criteria may evolve as the global music landscape continues to shift, potentially opening doors for more multilingual projects in future cycles.

Looking ahead, the upcoming Grammy nomination announcements will not only set a precedent for the Asian‑pop category but also signal how the Recording Academy intends to recognize the region’s burgeoning influence on worldwide music trends. Whether IU, Kenshi Yonezu, WayV, MILD, or Moira Dela Torre secures a spot, the first batch of nominees will likely shape the narrative for Asian artists seeking validation on one of the industry’s most prestigious stages, and could pave the way for an increasingly inclusive Grammy roster in the years to come.
